Con [[maq-puertas|las puertas]] se const: With [[maq-puertas|the gates]] any table can be built, and in [[lg-proposiciones|logic]] you already saw that a condition is a proposition. What is missing is what seems impossible in a circuit: deciding. A program writes “if this happens, do that”, and here there is nothing of the sort.
Un circuito no tiene instrucciones ni or: A circuit has no instructions and no order. All its gates are switched on at once, always, and each wire has whatever value falls to it. You cannot “jump over” a piece or “not execute” a gate. And yet a computer decides continually. The way of achieving it is the same one a conjuror uses: compute everything, and then show only one thing.
El circuito que elige se llama <strong>m: The circuit that chooses is called a multiplexer. It has two data inputs, one control input and one output, and it does exactly this: if the control is 0 it puts out the first input, and if it is 1 the second.

It reads: “m is x-and-not-s, or y-and-s”.

Each branch switches itself off when it is not its turn: if $s = 0$, the second bracket is 0 whatever happens with $y$, and the first lets $x$ through. With $s = 1$ it is the other way round.

Notice what does not happen: both branches are always computed. If $y$ were the result of a hugely expensive calculation, that calculation would be done anyway, even though $s$ is 0 and its result is thrown away. A circuit saves itself no work.

The underlying reason is identical: it is cheaper to compute both branches and throw one away than to decide which to compute.

El multiplexor es la pieza que hace posi: The multiplexer is the piece that makes it possible for a processor to have instructions. Inside the machine there is a single adder, a single comparator and a single logic unit, and what decides which of their results comes out on the output wire is a multiplexer governed by the instruction code. Changing instruction does not change the circuit: it changes the control wire. That will be seen assembled in [[maq-cpu|the minimal machine]], and it is what lets the same piece of silicon add, subtract or compare according to what the order says.
La idea de calcularlo todo y elegir desp: The idea of computing everything and choosing afterwards is older than electronics. The relay telephone exchanges of the early twentieth century already had selector circuits that connected one line among several, and in fact it was while working with telephone relays that Claude Shannon realised that this was Boolean algebra. The name multiplexer comes precisely from telecommunications, where to multiplex is to put several signals down the same wire; in a logic circuit it is the same, with a control wire deciding whose turn it is to pass.
